newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds strengthen following budget speech.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds strengthen following budget speech.

text.p: Canadian bonds strengthened slightly following the release of the federal budget on Tuesday, though prices were still lower than Monday's closing levels.

"They're still up a little bit from before he started speaking but they're not going anywhere, but they're not selling off either," said Hank Cunningham, director of fixed income with First Marathon Securities. "There's no bad surprises here at all."
Canada's 30-year bond was trading down C$0.45 to C$113.95 from Monday's close to yield 6.886 percent.
The 30-year bond had been trading down C$0.53 to C$113.87 to yield 6.853 percent before the news and gained as much as C$0.20 immediately following release of the budget.

"It's relatively neutral news," said Rich Wylie, a fixed-income economist with TD Securities Inc. "The market is almost always relieved when there's no surpises. They like consistency and it certainly looks like that's what is being shown in the budget here.
The U.S. 30-year benchmark bond was trading down 7/32 to yield 6.55 percent. The spread between the benchmark bonds widened to 30 from 28 basis points at Monday's close.
The spread between the bonds was 31 basis points before Finance Minister Paul Martin presented the budget.

Bond analysts said the market was heartened by the fact that the budget contained only minor spending increases. While there were several new programs announced analysts said the level of new spending was minor.

"I really don't think there were any surprises in this. With most of the stuff we had a pretty good idea that we were going to see it," said TD Securities' Wylie. "They've got some minor spending increases but if you look at the total dollar value it's relatively low."
However, some analysts said the fact that Martin failed to lower his deficit target for next year or set a target to balance the budget could have a negative effect on bonds.

"I think where he did fail was in not revising next year's deficit (target). I think there were a number of people who were looking for that revision and any calls for the balanced budget to be pushed one year ahead are not confirmed by this budget. So there's a possibility the market could take this as a negative, offshore players could take this as a negative," said Andrew Pyle, head of fixed-income research with ABN AMRO Bank Canada.
Pyle characterized the gains in bond prices following the budget as "relief trade."
But overall, bond analysts described the budget as positive for fixed-income markets.

"All of us feared that there might be some tugs at the sleeves by some of the left-wing spenders," said First Marathon's Cunningham. "He's made some extremely conservative assumptions, we believe, with interest rates and growth that lead us to conclude he will continue to outperform his own targets."

In other prices, the Government of Canada's 7.0 percent bond due 2006 fell C$0.32 to C$106.03 from Monday to yield 6.167. The 10-year bond had been trading down C$0.48 to C$105.87 to yield 6.189 percent before the release of the budget.

The U.S. 10-year bond fell 2/32 to yield 6.28 percent. The negative spread between the bonds narrowed 11 basis points from 15 basis points at the close of trading on Monday. The spread had narrowed to nine basis points before the budget.
The three-month cash T-bill traded with a yield of 2.89 percent against the U.S. bill which yielded 5.12 percent.
